stem: In which year was the Southern African Development Coordination Conference (SADCC) founded?

options.rationale: Correct: at Lusaka on 1 April 1980.
This is the year of the founding of the OAU.
This is the year in which SADC replaced SADCC.
This is the year in which the African Union was launched.

explanation: SADCC was founded at Lusaka on 1 April 1980.

stem: What was the main aim of SADCC when it was formed?

options.content: To reduce dependence on apartheid South Africa
options.rationale: Correct: it focused on transport, energy and food projects.

options.content: To create a single currency for the whole of southern Africa at once
options.rationale: A currency union was not an early aim.

options.content: To form a military alliance that would invade South Africa
options.rationale: SADCC was an economic body.

options.content: To join the countries of Europe in a customs union straight away
options.rationale: It was a regional body of African states.

explanation: SADCC aimed to reduce dependence on South Africa and to co-ordinate development projects.

stem: Where is the Secretariat of SADC located?

options.content: Harare, in Zimbabwe
options.rationale: ARIPO is headquartered in Harare, not SADC.

options.content: Lusaka, in Zambia
options.rationale: Lusaka hosted the founding summit of 1980.

options.content: Gaborone, in Botswana
options.rationale: Correct: it has been there since 1982.

options.content: Pretoria, in South Africa
options.rationale: South Africa joined SADC only in 1994.

explanation: The Secretariat is in Gaborone, Botswana.

stem: Which change from SADCC to SADC does the Windhoek Treaty of 1992 represent?

options.content: From a community with a treaty to an informal meeting of foreign ministers
options.rationale: SADC was the more formal body.

options.content: From a conference co-ordinating projects to a community aiming at integration
options.rationale: Correct: it created a legal community.

options.content: From a body based in Gaborone to a new body based in the city of Windhoek
options.rationale: The Secretariat stayed in Gaborone.

options.content: From a body of nine states to a group of exactly the same nine states
options.rationale: Membership grew.

explanation: SADC was a treaty-based community with the aim of deeper integration; SADCC had been a conference for co-ordinating projects.
hints: The new name used 'community' instead of 'conference'.

stem: What is the difference between a free trade area and a customs union?

options.content: A free trade area allows free movement of labour, but a customs union does not
options.rationale: That describes a common market.

options.content: A customs union adds a common external tariff to the removal of tariffs inside
options.rationale: Correct: members also share a tariff on outside goods.

options.content: A customs union has no tariffs at all, but a free trade area has high tariffs
options.rationale: Neither description is correct.

options.content: A free trade area is a political union with one government for all members
options.rationale: That describes political union.

explanation: Both remove tariffs among members; a customs union also adopts a common tariff on imports from outside.
hints: Think about what members do about imports from outside the group.

stem: Why did the end of apartheid change the purpose of regional co-operation in southern Africa?

options.content: South Africa declared war on all of its neighbours in the year 1994 and the region split
options.rationale: South Africa joined SADC in 1994.

options.content: Every member left SADCC and the whole organisation was abolished outright in 1990
options.rationale: SADCC became SADC.

options.content: The aim of reducing dependence on South Africa lost its basis, so integration became the goal
options.rationale: Correct: South Africa joined SADC in 1994.

options.content: Namibia became part of South Africa and left the region for good in the early 1990s
options.rationale: Namibia became independent in 1990.

explanation: With apartheid ending, regional co-operation shifted from opposing South African dominance to integration including South Africa.
hints: Think of South Africa joining SADC.

stem: Which of these is a problem that has slowed SADC integration?

options.content: The fact that all members have economies of exactly the same size
options.rationale: Economies differ widely in size.

options.content: The absence of any shared border between two members
options.rationale: Many members share borders.

options.content: The refusal of every member to attend meetings of the Summit
options.rationale: The Summit meets each year.

options.content: Overlapping membership of groupings such as COMESA and the EAC
options.rationale: Correct: it complicates tariffs and rules.

explanation: Overlapping memberships, the dominance of South Africa's economy, poor infrastructure and political differences have slowed integration.
hints: Think about members who belong to several groups.

stem: Which point best supports the view that SADC has made progress towards integration?

options.content: The customs union that was planned for 2010 has still not been completed by members
options.rationale: This shows delay, not progress.

options.content: Members belong to several overlapping groups with different rules and tariffs
options.rationale: This shows a problem.

options.content: South Africa's economy is much larger than those of most of the other members
options.rationale: This shows a difficulty.

options.content: A Free Trade Area was launched in 2008, removing most tariffs among participants
options.rationale: Correct: it shows a real stage achieved.

explanation: The launch of the Free Trade Area in 2008 was a concrete step; the customs union and later stages have been delayed.

stem: SADCC had nine founding member states in 1980.
explanation: The nine were Angola, Botswana, Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Swaziland, Tanzania, Zambia and Zimbabwe.

explanation: SADCC was decentralised: Zimbabwe co-ordinated food security, Mozambique transport and communications, and Angola energy.

stem:
Study the sources and answer the questions.

**Source A** — an extract from a speech by a fictional southern African leader at a summit in 1981 (invented for this question)

> Our railways run to the south because the old masters laid them so. We shall lay new lines to our own ports, share our electricity, and feed ourselves. Let no one say that we are poor; we are dependent, and dependence can be ended.

**Source B** — a report by a fictional economist for a regional business association, 2012 (invented for this question)

> The tariffs among our members have fallen, but trade among us is still a small share of our total trade. A trader may be asked to follow three sets of rules for one consignment, and roads and border posts remain slow. Integration on paper is not yet integration in practice.

points.description: Agree that co-operation aims to link the economies of the region and reduce external dependence
Differ in tone: A is confident about ending dependence; B reports slow progress in practice
Provenance: A is a political speech at the beginning of SADCC; B an economist's report thirty years later

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The sources agree that regional co-operation is meant to link the economies of the region and reduce dependence. They differ in tone and time. Source A, a political speech at the beginning of SADCC, is confident that dependence can be ended, while Source B, an economist's report thirty years later, shows that trade among members is small and the rules and roads are still a problem. My own knowledge supports both: SADCC improved transport corridors, and SADC launched a free trade area in 2008, but the customs union has been delayed.

explanation: Both sources are invented: a leader's speech and an economist's report.
hints: For (c), notice that the sources are written about thirty years apart.

stem: To what extent has SADC been successful in promoting regional co-operation and integration since 1992?

points.description: Aims and stages: Windhoek Treaty, RISDP, free trade area, customs union, common market, monetary union
Achievements: Free Trade Area in 2008, protocols, power pool, infrastructure such as Kazungula, mediation, health and food programmes
Problems: South Africa's dominance, overlapping memberships, infrastructure, political differences, dependence on donors, delays
Comparison with SADCC or with other regional groupings
Supported judgement

levels.descriptor: Developed, well-supported explanation of several relevant factors or arguments, using accurate and specific knowledge, weighing them against each other and against alternative views, with a sustained line of argument and a supported judgement that answers the question.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; limited balance and little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: SADC has been partly successful. Its Windhoek Treaty of 1992 set the aim of deeper integration, and the RISDP set stages leading from a free trade area to a customs union, a common market and monetary union. A free trade area was launched in 2008 and most tariffs among participating members were removed, and SADC has agreed protocols on trade, gender and shared resources, built regional infrastructure such as the Kazungula Bridge and the power pool, and played a role in mediation in places such as Madagascar and Lesotho. But the customs union has been delayed, the dominance of South Africa's economy, overlapping memberships, poor infrastructure and political differences have slowed progress, and trade among members is still a small part of their total trade. I conclude that SADC has achieved more than the loose co-operation of SADCC, especially in infrastructure and trade rules, but its deeper integration targets have not been met.

explanation: Credit aims, achievements, problems, comparison and a supported judgement.
hints: Compare the targets for integration with what has been achieved.

stem: Assess the importance of Zimbabwe in the work of SADCC in the 1980s.

points.description: Founding role and the sector for food security in Harare
Defence of the transport links, such as the Beira Corridor, and the support of the Frontline States
Limits: Zimbabwe's own dependence on South African routes, the cost of the war in Mozambique, and the small size of the region's economies
Judgement on how important Zimbabwe's role was

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Zimbabwe played an important role in SADCC in the 1980s. It was a founder member and co-ordinated the food security sector from Harare, and it helped to defend the Beira Corridor, which gave land-locked states a route to the sea outside South Africa. But Zimbabwe itself still depended on South African routes, the cost of the Mozambique operation was heavy, and the region's economies were small. I conclude that Zimbabwe was among the most important members, because of its relatively strong economy and its commitment to the transport links, but it could not by itself end the region's dependence.

explanation: Credit explained role, limits and a judgement.
hints: Link Zimbabwe's role to the aims of SADCC.
